h1: Why strong lager sells so well on Indian beer shelves
title: Why Strong Lager Leads in India | Craft Beer School
desc: Why strong lager dominates Indian beer sales: tax, value, taste, chilling and habit, plus what that means for anyone building a beer brand.
teaser: Walk into any Indian liquor shop and the strong beers own the fridge. That is not an accident.
standfirst: Strong lager outsells every other beer style on Indian shelves. Understanding why, from excise design to the way people drink, matters for anyone trying to launch, position or price a beer brand here.
sections: What strong beer means in India

In India, strong beer usually means a lager above 5% ABV, often in the 6 to 8% range. Mild or regular beer sits below 5%. Most states treat the two as separate categories for excise, labelling and pricing, though the exact thresholds and rules vary by state.

Strong lager is the main event for the large brewing companies. It is bright, pale, fizzy and served very cold, much like an American light lager in appearance, but with noticeably more alcohol and sweetness.
Reason one: alcohol for the rupee

Many Indian drinkers compare beer not with other beers but with spirits. Whisky and other spirits make up the larger part of alcohol drunk in India. A drinker choosing between a quarter bottle of whisky and a couple of beers often thinks in terms of how much alcohol each rupee buys.

A strong lager gives more alcohol per bottle than a mild one, often at a small price difference. For a price-conscious buyer that is a simple calculation.
Reason two: how excise is structured

Beer excise in India is set by each state. The structure matters. Some states have historically levied duty by bulk litre or on price slabs rather than strictly on alcohol content. Where duty does not rise much with ABV, a stronger beer carries little extra tax per unit of alcohol, which makes strong beer the better value for the brewer and the buyer.

Other states tax by strength or price in ways that change the picture. Rules are revised often. Our guide to beer excise duty in India explains the main models. Anyone building a pricing plan should check the current notifications in each state they sell in, ideally with a licensing or excise adviser.
Reason three: the taste and the serve

Strong lager is brewed to be drunk ice cold. At 2 to 4 °C, alcohol warmth and sweetness are muted. The beer tastes smooth rather than boozy. In a hot climate, a very cold, sweetish, high strength beer is easy to drink.

The large breweries often make it using high gravity brewing: they brew a concentrated wort, ferment it and dilute to the target strength. They usually include adjuncts like rice, maize or sugar, which lighten the body and keep the flavour clean. The result is consistent, inexpensive to make at scale and tuned to local preference for a slightly sweet finish.
Reason four: habit and the occasion

A lot of beer in India is drunk in social settings where people share large bottles. The 650 ml bottle is a familiar format, often shared between friends or with food. A strong beer in that format suits an evening's drinking at a pace many groups are used to.

Brands also built strong lager around masculine, robust imagery for decades. Repeated over years in shops and bars, that positioning shaped what many drinkers think a beer should be. Alcohol advertising is restricted in India, so brand familiarity has often been built through surrogate products, packaging and presence on shelves rather than direct campaigns.
What this means if you are building a brand

For a craft brewer or a new beer brand, strong lager is the benchmark you are being compared with, whether you like it or not. Three practical points follow:

  • Price against value, not just quality. A drinker used to strong lager will notice if your 4.5% beer costs more and gives less alcohol. Explain what else they get: flavour, freshness, a local story.
  • Do not ignore the strong segment. Some craft brewers have found success with stronger styles such as Belgian ales, double IPAs or strong wheat beers, which offer flavour and alcohol together.
  • Know your excise. Strength thresholds can change the tax band and label requirements. Recipe and pricing decisions should be made together, not in separate rooms.

Tastes are moving, slowly. Younger urban drinkers in the big cities increasingly try wheat beers, IPAs and lower alcohol options. Premium mild beers have grown in visibility. Our guide to craft beer market trends in India looks at where that is heading.

Strong lager will stay a large part of the market for a long time. The opportunity for new brands lies in understanding exactly why people buy it, then offering a reason to try something else that respects those reasons rather than dismissing them.
faqs: What ABV counts as strong beer in India?
Generally above 5% ABV, though thresholds and categories differ by state. Most strong lagers on Indian shelves sit between about 6 and 8%.
Is strong lager taxed more than mild beer?
It depends on the state. Some excise structures barely change with strength, while others tax stronger beer more. Rules change often, so check the current state notification.
Why is strong lager sweeter than mild lager?
Higher gravity brewing leaves more residual sugar. Brewers often tune the finish to local taste. Serving it ice cold also changes how the sweetness and alcohol come across.
Should a craft brand make a strong beer?
It can, if it fits the brand. Stronger styles with real flavour can appeal to drinkers used to strong lager, but price, excise band and labelling must be planned together.
